Clara’s breath caught in her throat, a little knot of fear and wonder. ‘It is the Sunken Garden you speak of,’ she said, her voice barely a whisper. ‘Yes, the Garden. To be at one with the water must be the most profound peace. To feel the cool green weeds as a blanket, and watch the silent dance of the fish above. To have no memory of the sun, and no longing for the moon. To forget joy, to forgive sorrow, to be finally still. It is you who can help me. You can unlatch the gate to my long slumber, for you carry the key of Kindness, and Kindness is more patient than Time is.’ A tremor passed through Clara, and for a moment the gaslit library seemed to sway around her. The world felt thin, like old paper. Then the Lady of the Lake spoke again, her voice like the shifting of pebbles under a slow current. ‘Have you not seen the inscription on the old astrolabe?’ ‘Many times,’ cried the girl, her eyes wide; ‘I have traced the letters with my finger. They are etched in tarnished silver, and the script is strange. It reads: When the last son of the line Renounces what is his by right, When a maiden’s heart, so fine, Shares a flicker of its light, Then the waters will recede And the ancient pact be freed. But I have never understood its meaning.’ ‘It means,’ the spirit murmured with a deep sigh, ‘that you must give to me a memory you have cherished, for my own are all washed away, and you must feel for my loneliness one moment of true pity, for I have forgotten how to feel. And then, if your heart has always been true, the Guardian of the Garden will grant me passage. You will hear the whispers of the drowned, and feel the pull of the deep, but they cannot touch you, for against the warmth of a living soul the cold of the past has no power.’ Clara did not reply, and the Lady wrung her spectral hands, her form wavering like a reflection in a disturbed pool. Then, with a sudden intake of breath, the girl stood tall, her face pale but resolute. ‘I am not afraid,’ she declared, ‘and I will give you my memory of the summer fair.’ A soft cry, like the sound of a distant bell, escaped the Lady’s lips. She drifted forward and took Clara’s hand; her touch was like cool spring water, and her lips, as she brushed them against the girl’s knuckles, felt like the mist from a waterfall. On the great tapestry that depicted the founding of the house, the woven ladies in waiting turned their silken heads. They raised their hands in warning and their stitched mouths opened. ‘Do not go! sweet Clara,’ they seemed to plead, ‘do not go!’ but the spirit’s grip was firm, and Clara closed her eyes to their silent entreaty. Strange creatures with the fins of fish and the eyes of owls, carved into the great oak mantelpiece, seemed to stir in the firelight and croak, ‘Beware! sweet Clara, beware! the garden keeps what it is given,’ but the Lady only moved more swiftly, and Clara would not hear them. When they came to the far end of the library, she stopped and sang a single, clear note that shivered in the air. Clara opened her eyes to see the bookshelf swinging inwards, revealing not a passage, but a great, round window of solid, rippling water. A damp, mossy wind gusted out, carrying the scent of river mud and rain. ‘Hurry, hurry,’ the Lady urged, ‘before the tide turns,’ and in an instant, the bookshelf had swung shut behind them, and the library was once again silent.

CHAPTER IV

Scarcely a quarter of an hour had passed when the bell was rung for evening prayers, and, as Clara did not appear, Mrs. Blackwood sent the parlourmaid to fetch her. In a short while the maid returned, her face a mask of confusion, and announced that she could not find Miss Clara at all. As it was her custom to walk by the ornamental ponds before dusk, Mrs. Blackwood was not unduly alarmed, but when nine o’clock struck from the grandfather clock in the hall, and Clara had still not returned, a genuine panic began to set in. She sent the boys to search the grounds, while she and Mr. Blackwood began a thorough canvass of the house. At half-past nine the boys returned, breathless and cold, reporting that there was no sign of their sister anywhere. The entire household was now in a state of considerable consternation, and no one knew what to do, when Mr. Blackwood suddenly recalled that a troupe of travelling players had been given leave to make camp in the east meadow. He at once set out for the meadow, his eldest son, Arthur, and two of the gardeners accompanying him. Young Lord Harrington, who had been dining with them and was now in a state of abject misery, begged to be allowed to come, but Mr. Blackwood refused, as he thought the players might be a rough sort. Upon reaching the meadow, however, he found the players had already departed; their exit had clearly been made in some haste, for a costume trunk lay open and a few painted props were scattered on the ground. Having sent Arthur and the gardeners to check the road to the village, he hurried back to the house and dispatched telegrams to the constabulary in three counties, alerting them to a possible abduction by theatrical vagrants. He then had his horse saddled, and, after ordering his wife and the two younger boys to take some soup, he rode off towards the old Roman road with a groom. He had not gone more than three miles, however, when he heard the frantic drumming of hooves behind him, and, turning, saw young Lord Harrington approaching on his chestnut mare, his riding coat unbuttoned and his hair in disarray. ‘I beg your pardon, Mr. Blackwood,’ the young man panted, ‘but I cannot possibly touch soup while Clara is missing. Please, do not be cross with me; had you permitted our engagement this spring, I should have been here to look after her. You will not send me back, will you? I cannot bear it! I will not bear it!’ The master of the house could not help but smile at the handsome, distraught young man, and he was quite moved by his earnestness, so leaning over in his saddle, he clapped him on the shoulder and said, ‘Very well, James, if you will not be sent back, you must ride with me, but I insist you button your coat against the night air.’ ‘Oh, a pox on my coat! We must find Clara!’ cried the young Lord, a hysterical laugh escaping him, and they spurred their horses onward to the crossroads. There Mr. Blackwood questioned the toll-keeper whether a carriage or anyone matching Clara’s description had passed, but he had seen nothing. The toll-keeper, however, promised to send word down the line with the morning mail-coach, and, after thanking him, Mr. Blackwood rode on to Oakhaven, a small hamlet known for its disreputable inn, as he was told the players were fond of stopping there. They roused the publican, but could learn nothing from him, and after searching the inn’s common room, they turned their horses for home, arriving at the estate at well past midnight, bone-weary and with heavy hearts. They saw Arthur and the twins waiting by the main gate with lanterns, for the long drive was shrouded in fog. No trace of Clara had been found. The players had been located in the next town, but she was not among them, and they explained their hasty departure by claiming they had misremembered the dates of the market fair and were in a rush. They professed great shock at hearing of Clara’s disappearance, for they were very grateful to Mr. Blackwood for the use of his meadow, and two of their men had volunteered to join the search. The ornamental ponds had been dragged, and the entire estate gone over, but to no avail. It was quite clear that, for this night at least, Clara was truly gone; and it was in a state of the most profound gloom that Mr. Blackwood and the boys walked back to the house, the groom following with the tired horses. In the entrance hall, they were met by a huddle of anxious servants, and laid out on a chaise-longue in the drawing-room was poor Mrs. Blackwood, quite beside herself with grief and worry, while the old housekeeper bathed her temples with lavender water. Mr. Blackwood immediately insisted she have something to eat, and had a supper of cold meats and bread laid for the entire party. It was a melancholy meal, for no one said a word, and even the twins were pale and quiet, as they were deeply fond of their sister. When they had finished, there was nothing to do but wait for the dawn.

When they had finished, there was nothing to do but wait for the dawn.

Mr. Blackwood suggested they all retire to the drawing-room, for the dining hall felt unnaturally cold and vast without Clara’s bright presence at the table. Mrs. Blackwood, who had barely touched the food placed before her, was led to the sofa, where she lay with a scented handkerchief pressed to her eyes, her silent sobs shaking her slender frame from time to time. The twins, for the first time in their lives seemingly devoid of any spirit for mischief, sat together on a small ottoman by the unlit hearth, their faces pale and their eyes wide with a fear they did not fully comprehend. Arthur, ever the responsible eldest, stood by the window, peering out into the impenetrable fog as if his sheer force of will might part it and reveal his sister walking up the drive.

Only young Lord James seemed incapable of stillness. He paced the length of the great Axminster carpet, his hands clenched behind his back, his riding boots making no sound on the thick pile. Every few moments he would stop, listen intently for a sound that never came, and then resume his restless march. His handsome face was a mask of anguish, and his usually immaculate hair was dishevelled.

‘We should not have come back,’ he said suddenly, his voice rough with emotion. ‘We should have kept searching. She could be anywhere, cold, frightened…’

‘James, my boy, we have done all that can be done for tonight,’ Mr. Blackwood replied, his own voice heavy with exhaustion. He had placed himself in a large armchair opposite his wife, his posture that of a captain on the bridge of a sinking ship. ‘The entire district is on alert. Every constable, every station-master for twenty miles knows to look for her. To wander aimlessly in this fog would be folly. We must conserve our strength for the morning.’

‘The morning!’ exclaimed James, turning on him with a wild look in his eyes. ‘How can we speak of the morning when Clara is lost to us now? Every minute that passes is an eternity of torment!’ He ran a hand through his hair in despair. ‘I cannot simply sit here and wait. It is unendurable.’

‘Nevertheless, you must,’ said Mr. Blackwood, his tone firm but not unkind. ‘For Mrs. Blackwood’s sake, and for your own. Panicking will not help Clara.’

Young Lord James fell silent at the mention of Mrs. Blackwood, casting a pained glance at her trembling form on the sofa. He ceased his pacing and went to join Arthur at the window, two sentinels staring out into a void of grey mist. The only sound in the room was the solemn ticking of the great grandfather clock in the hall, each second falling like a drop of water in the vast, silent pool of their shared anxiety. The fire had died down to sullen embers, and a chill began to creep into the room, a chill that had nothing to do with the night air.

The hours wore on. Ten o’clock became eleven, and eleven began its slow march toward midnight. The servants, who had been hovering with anxious faces in the hall, were dismissed to their beds, though it was doubtful any of them would sleep. Mr. Blackwood persuaded his wife to take a small glass of brandy, and the old housekeeper helped her upstairs, murmuring words of comfort. The twins finally succumbed to exhaustion, falling asleep huddled together on the ottoman, their faces tear-streaked even in slumber.

Just as the great clock in the hall began to chime the hour of midnight, a most peculiar thing occurred. It did not strike with its usual deep and sonorous toll, but with a jarring, discordant clang, as if a string inside its ancient works had snapped. The twelfth stroke was followed not by silence, but by a low, drawn-out groan that seemed to emanate from the very walls of the house. A gust of wind, cold and smelling of damp earth and faded lilies, swept through the drawing-room, extinguishing the last of the lamps and plunging them into near total darkness, save for the faint moonlight that now, strangely, began to filter through the fog outside.

At the same instant, a sudden grinding noise was heard from the far end of the hall, a sound of stone grating against stone that made them all start to their feet. Mr. Blackwood snatched a lantern that one of the boys had left on a side-table, and fumbled to light it.

‘What in heaven’s name was that?’ he muttered, his hand trembling slightly as the wick caught flame.

Arthur and James rushed out of the drawing-room into the hall, with Mr. Blackwood following close behind. The lantern cast huge, dancing shadows up the grand staircase and across the walls. The noise had come from the wall beside the staircase, from a large, dark panel of oak that was supposed to be merely decorative. But it was not a panel any more; it was a dark, gaping aperture, a black doorway that had not been there a moment before.

And there, framed in the dark aperture, stood Clara.

She was very pale, but her eyes, which seemed enormous in the lantern light, held a strange and luminous calm. Her golden hair was slightly disarrayed, but her dress was immaculate. In her hands she carried a small, intricately carved oaken box.

For a moment, no one moved or spoke. They simply stared, as if at an apparition. Then, with a choked cry, young Lord James sprang forward. ‘Clara!’

He fell to his knees before her, seizing her hand and covering it with kisses, his shoulders shaking with relief. ‘Clara, you are safe! We thought… we feared… oh, my darling!’

Her name on his lips broke the spell. Mr. Blackwood let out a great, shuddering breath and hurried to her, while Arthur ran back to the drawing-room crying, ‘She’s here! She’s back!’

‘Clara, my child, where have you been?’ Mr. Blackwood demanded, his voice a mixture of overwhelming relief and stern paternal authority. ‘We have been half-mad with worry. The whole county is out looking for you! Were you kidnapped? Did those players take you?’

Clara looked down at the distraught young man at her feet, and then at her father’s anxious face. A faint, sad smile touched her lips. She placed a gentle hand on James’s head.

‘I am quite well, Father,’ she said, and her voice was strangely altered. It was still her own sweet voice, but it held a new depth, a new maturity, as if she had aged years in the few hours she had been gone. ‘No one harmed me. I have been with Sir Geoffrey.’

Mr. Blackwood stared at her blankly. ‘Sir Geoffrey? Who is Sir Geoffrey? One of the players?’

‘No,’ she said softly. ‘The ghost.’

A profound silence fell upon the hall. Arthur had returned with the twins, who were rubbing the sleep from their eyes, but even they were struck dumb by this pronouncement.

‘Clara, my dear child,’ said Mr. Blackwood, stepping forward, his practical American mind struggling to grasp the fantastical tale, ‘you have been through a terrible ordeal. You are overwrought. There are no such things as ghosts.’

‘Oh, but there are,’ Clara insisted, her gaze unwavering. ‘Or at least, there was. He is at peace now, Father. That is where I have been. I have helped him to find his rest.’

She then proceeded to tell them the most extraordinary story. She told them how the ghost of Sir Geoffrey Blackwood, who had murdered his wife in a fit of jealous rage three hundred years ago and had been starved to death by her brothers in retribution, had appeared to her in the Portrait Gallery. He had spoken to her of his long, weary torment, of his desperate longing for the peace of the Garden of Death. He had shown her the old prophecy carved on the mantelpiece, a prophecy that foretold his release.

‘“When a maiden fair of heart,”’ Clara recited, her voice a low whisper in the cavernous hall, ‘“Can bid a sinner’s tears to start, When the blighted yew-tree thrives, And a gentle soul forgives past lives, Then the house shall quiet be, And Blackwood’s spirit shall be free.” But he could not weep, for his heart was withered, and he could not pray, for he had lost his faith. He asked me,’ her voice trembled slightly, ‘he asked me to weep for him, and to pray for his soul.’

James had risen to his feet and now stood beside her, his arm protectively around her shoulders, his face a study in wonder and adoration.

‘He led me through the wall,’ Clara continued, gesturing to the open panel. ‘Into the darkness. I saw dreadful things there, Father, terrible shapes that whispered from the shadows, but they could not touch me. Sir Geoffrey said that the innocence of a child was a shield that the forces of darkness could not breach. He led me to a small, hidden chamber, his own secret prison. And there… there he asked me to kneel and pray for all the sins of his life. And as I wept for his sorrow, the blighted old yew-tree outside the window, the one the gardeners said was dead, burst into bloom with white flowers. It was the sign. The curse was broken.’

She paused, and a single tear traced a path down her pale cheek. ‘Then the Angel of Death came for him. It was not frightening, but beautiful. He looked so happy, so peaceful. He thanked me, and then… he was gone.’

Mr. Blackwood listened to this incredible narrative with a deep frown on his face. He looked from his daughter’s earnest, shining eyes to the black opening in the wall, and then back again. ‘Clara,’ he said slowly, ‘you are telling me that you voluntarily went with a three-hundred-year-old spectre into a secret passage because he asked you to?’

‘Yes, Father,’ she replied simply.

‘And that this… this ghost is now gone to his eternal rest?’

‘Yes. His bones are in the secret chamber. He can finally sleep.’

Mr. Blackwood was a man who believed in facts, in ledgers, in tangible evidence. He did not believe in prophecies or spectres. And yet, here was his daughter, who had vanished from a locked room, reappearing through a solid wall with a story that, while utterly insane, she clearly believed with all her heart.

‘Show me,’ he said, his voice resolute. ‘Show me this chamber.’

Clara nodded. ‘Of course, Father. But you must be quiet and respectful. It is a place of great sorrow.’

Taking up the lantern, Mr. Blackwood motioned for the others to follow. James kept a firm hold of Clara’s hand, as if afraid she might vanish again. Arthur and the twins followed behind, their earlier fear now replaced by a sense of profound and solemn awe. They stepped through the dark opening in the wall. A narrow, stone staircase spiralled downwards into utter blackness. A damp, earthy smell met them, the scent of centuries of undisturbed stillness.

The stairs ended in a short, narrow corridor, and at the end of the corridor was a low, iron-studded door. It was not locked. Clara pushed it open, and they entered a small, windowless cell, hewn from the very foundations of the house.

The lantern light fell upon a grim and pitiable sight. Chained by the wrist and ankle to a great iron ring set in the wall was a human skeleton, which had collapsed into a heap on the stone floor. The chains were thick with rust, and the bones were yellowed with age. Beside the skeleton lay a broken earthenware jug and a wooden platter, now little more than a disc of crumbling dust. It was the skeleton of a tall man, and on the stone floor, scattered around it as if they had just fallen, were the petals of fresh, white yew-blossoms.

A collective gasp went through the small group. The twins shrank back behind Arthur, their eyes wide with terror. Mr. Blackwood, the great sceptic, stood frozen, the lantern held high, his face a mask of disbelief. Everything his daughter had said was true.

Clara knelt beside the skeletal remains, her expression one of immense pity. ‘He was so tired,’ she whispered.

After a long, stunned silence, Mr. Blackwood finally spoke, his voice hushed. ‘We must… we must give him a proper burial.’

He turned to leave the dreadful place, but Clara remained, looking down at the small oaken box she still held in her hands.

‘What is that, my dear?’ Mr. Blackwood asked, his tone now gentle and full of a new respect for his daughter.

‘It was his last gift to me,’ Clara said, and with trembling fingers, she lifted the lid.

Inside, nestled upon a bed of faded black velvet, lay a trove of magnificent jewels. They flashed and glittered in the lantern light, casting brilliant flecks of colour onto the grim stone walls. There were ropes of pearls, a great ruby pendant that seemed to pulse with an inner fire, diamond buckles, and a necklace of square-cut emeralds, each one perfect and of the deepest green. They were jewels of an ancient and fabulous design, clearly worth a fortune.

‘Good heavens,’ murmured Mr. Blackwood, his business instincts momentarily overriding his awe. ‘Those must be the Blackwood family jewels. They were thought to be lost for centuries.’ He looked at Clara. ‘My dear, as they were found on this property, I believe they legally belong to the estate.’

‘No, Father,’ Clara said firmly, looking up at him. Her eyes flashed with a spirit he had never seen in her before. ‘They do not belong to the estate. They belong to me. They were a gift from Sir Geoffrey, a thank you for my tears. He told me so himself.’

Before Mr. Blackwood could formulate a reply to this rather unbusinesslike claim, young Lord James stepped forward. ‘She is right, sir,’ he said, his voice ringing with conviction. ‘No one can claim a gift given in gratitude for such a service. These jewels are Clara’s, and hers alone.’ He smiled down at her. ‘Though I fancy they are not half so bright as her own heart.’

Mr. Blackwood looked at his daughter, so pale and yet so resolute, and at the handsome young lord standing guard over her, and he felt his practical objections melting away. He had gotten his daughter back, and in the process, the house had been freed of its ancient curse. A few antique trinkets seemed a small price to pay.

‘Very well, Clara,’ he said, with a slight smile. ‘The jewels are yours.’

He then took charge, as was his way. He sent Arthur to wake the groom and have him ride to the police station at Oakhaven to call off the search, with instructions to be as discreet as possible about the reasons for Clara’s reappearance. He sent the twins, now thoroughly subdued, off to bed with a stern command not to breathe a word of what they had seen.

A few days later, a small, private funeral was held in a quiet corner of the churchyard. In a new coffin lay the earthly remains of Sir Geoffrey Blackwood. The entire family attended, along with a deeply moved Lord James. As the vicar read the last rites, Clara stepped forward and placed the oaken box of jewels upon the coffin, intending for it to be buried with him.

But James gently stopped her, taking her hand. ‘He would not want that, Clara,’ he whispered. ‘He gave them to you so that you might know a life of brightness and joy, not to return them to the darkness. His freedom was your gift to him; these are his to you.’

He reached into the box and took out a single, slender gold chain, which he fastened around her neck. ‘Keep them,’ he said. ‘And wear them, and remember the sad ghost who is now at peace because of your goodness.’

Clara nodded, her eyes filling with tears once more, but this time they were not tears of sorrow.

And from that day forward, the Blackwood ghost was never seen again. The strange bloodstain in the library, which had so vexed Mrs. Blackwood, faded away completely, and the house was filled with a newfound sense of peace and light. The twins, having been profoundly affected by the events of that night, gave up their pranks entirely and became remarkably well behaved. And when, in the following spring, Clara Blackwood was married to Lord James, her only ornaments were the magnificent Blackwood emeralds, which shone no less brightly than the happy, loving light in her eyes. The Minister, in giving her away, was heard to remark to a guest that he was all for free trade and free institutions, but that he had to admit there was a great deal to be said for the English aristocracy, after all.

Arthur, ever the responsible eldest, stood by the window, peering out into the impenetrable fog as if his sheer force of will might part it and reveal his sister walking up the drive.

Every few moments he would stop, listen intently for a sound that never came, and then resume his restless march. It was the skeleton of a tall man, and on the stone floor, scattered around it as if they had just fallen, were the petals of fresh, white yew-blossoms.

‘It was his last gift to me,’ Clara said, and with trembling fingers, she lifted the lid.

The Ghost of Canterville was never seen again, but the memory of him, and the great lesson of his peace, lived on, a strange and beautiful legend in the annals of a very old family and a very new one.

She stood there, pale but composed, her hands clasped before her. There were no tears on her face, but her blue eyes shone with a curious light, not of fear, but of profound and solemn knowledge. She looked as if she had just returned from a long journey and had witnessed things that words could not describe. ‘Virginia!’ The cry was a chorus of relief and disbelief.

Mrs. Otis was the first to reach her, gathering her into her arms and covering her face with kisses. ‘Oh, my child, my darling child! Where have you been? We thought we had lost you forever!’

She looked down at the casket in her hands. ‘He asked me to weep for him, because his heart had been sealed for three hundred years and he could not. He asked me to pray for him, because his soul had forgotten how. I went with him to the Garden of Death.’

‘The Garden of Death!’ gasped Mrs. Otis, clutching her heart.

‘Yes,’ said Virginia, a faint, sad smile touching her lips. ‘It is not a terrible place. It is very quiet. The Ghost is sleeping there now. He said that Death was only a brother to Sleep, and that he had been so very, very tired. Before he lay down to rest, he gave me this.’

‘No, Papa,’ Virginia said firmly. ‘You cannot. They were a gift. Sir Simon told me that they were a poor recompense for what he had cost me, but that in my hands they would be safe. They led the entire family out to the long, dark avenue of yew-trees. There, standing at the end of the walk, was the old, barren almond-tree. For as long as anyone could remember, it had been a withered, lifeless skeleton of a tree. But now, overnight, it had burst into bloom. Every branch was covered in a profusion of delicate white and pink blossoms, which scented the air with a faint, sweet perfume.

‘The barren almond bears!’ cried Washington, in a tone of complete awe.

It was clear to them all that the ancient prophecy had been fulfilled in every detail. Peace had, at last, come to Canterville.

A few days later, a simple and solemn funeral was held. In a quiet corner of the churchyard, not far from the ancient yew-tree under which he had so often sat, the skeleton of Sir Simon de Canterville was laid to rest. The Otis family attended, along with the little Duke of Cheshire and Mrs. Umney. As the coffin was lowered into the ground, Virginia stepped forward and laid upon it the silver casket of jewels. It was her final farewell to the sad and lonely spirit who had taught her the great mystery of Life, the greater mystery of Death, and why Love is stronger than both.

As they walked back to the house, the little Duke slipped his hand into Virginia’s. ‘Virginia,’ he said, his voice very low and earnest, ‘now that you are safe, and the Ghost is at peace, my anxiety has returned, but it is of a different sort. Mr. Otis would not let me be engaged to you last year, for he said we were both too young. Perhaps now, he might reconsider? After all, you have communed with spirits and travelled to the Garden of Death. I do not think anyone could call you too young for marriage after that.’

Virginia did not answer, but she smiled at him, and did not pull her hand away.

That evening, as they all sat together in the library, a great sense of peace seemed to fill the ancient room. The blood-stain had been washed away for the final time and did not reappear. The suits of armour no longer creaked and groaned, and no ghostly laughter echoed in the corridors.

Mr. Otis, who had written a long and detailed letter to Lord Canterville explaining the entire series of events, was holding Virginia’s hand. ‘Well, Ginny,’ he said, with a smile, ‘I am not sure I approve of my daughter accepting jewellery from sixteenth-century spectres. It is highly irregular. However,’ he added, with a twinkle in his eye, ‘I have spoken with Cecil, and as he seems to have appointed himself your permanent protector, and as you seem not to object to the arrangement, your mother and I have decided that one cannot stand in the way of a devotion that has been tested by both gypsies and ghosts. Though I must say, I never thought when I bought Canterville Chase that I was acquiring a family curse and a titled son-in-law all as part of the purchase price.’

And so, Virginia received the Canterville jewels as her betrothal gift, and wore them at her wedding the following spring, at which she was the loveliest bride that England had seen in many a year. She and the Duke were deliriously happy, and though she never revealed to anyone the full details of what had passed between her and the Ghost in those lost hours, she would often take her husband to the quiet corner of the churchyard and speak to him of what Sir Simon had taught her. She had learned that Love, when it is pure and selfless, has the power to redeem even the most stained of souls, and that for every dark and haunted house in the world, there is a golden girl with a key of compassion, able to open the portals not only of Death’s house, but of Heaven’s, too. The Ghost of Canterville was never seen again, but the memory of him, and the great lesson of his peace, lived on, a strange and beautiful legend in the annals of a very old family and a very new one.

That evening, as Virginia sat with her husband in the twilight of the Tapestry Chamber, a faint, shimmering figure appeared before them. Mr. Otis, who had a robust faith in the efficacy of action, had exhausted all possible actions and was now left with the terrible and unfamiliar business of waiting. This is the Canterville inheritance!’ ‘They are your dowry, my dear,’ he said, turning to his daughter with a tear in his eye. ‘Though I must say, Sir Simon could have saved us all a great deal of trouble by simply leaving them on the mantelpiece.’ And so, the strange and terrible adventure of the Canterville Ghost came to an end. The Ghost was never seen again, and the blood-stain in the library, having been scrubbed one last time with Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent, faded at last and returned no more. Canterville Chase, for the first time in three hundred years, was well and truly at peace.

The twins, having been sent to Eton and then Oxford, where they astonished their tutors with their ingenuity in avoiding all forms of classical education, had embarked upon careers in the City, where their talent for disruption was, for the first time, handsomely rewarded. Washington had married a celebrated English beauty with a fortune even larger than his own, and had devoted himself to collecting rare books and cultivating an impressive collection of orchids. Mr. and Mrs. Otis, finding the English climate disagreed with them in the long run, eventually returned to America, leaving the Chase in the capable hands of their daughter and son-in-law. The ghosts, it seemed, were gone for good, and the only spirits to be found in the house were those poured into glasses at dinnertime.

It was this very peace that began to trouble the new Duke of Cheshire, who, despite his title and his newfound responsibilities, had never quite lost the mischievous spirit of his boyhood. ‘It is all very well, you know,’ he remarked one evening to Virginia, as they sat in the Great Hall, which was now brightly lit by electric lamps of Mr. Otis’s own design. ‘But the place has become dreadfully respectable. ‘Cecil, don’t be absurd,’ said Virginia, though she smiled as she said it. ‘Poor Sir Simon earned his rest. And think of the servants; Cook was threatening to leave every other week.’

‘I know, I know,’ he sighed, ‘but it was an adventure. Now all we have to look forward to are county fairs and visits from my great-aunt. And she is far more terrifying than Sir Simon ever was, I can tell you.’

It did not start with a blood-stain or a groan, but with a subtle and pervasive scent of potpourri, of a kind that had not been fashionable for at least fifty years, that seemed to emanate from the Queen Anne suite. Then, the Blue Bedchamber, a room notorious for its dampness, suddenly became the warmest and driest room in the house, its curtains perpetually drawn against the midday sun. The manifestations are benign, almost… fussy. It is a domestic haunting. A haunting of tidiness.’

The twins, who had come down for the weekend, were delighted. ‘I say, Stripes,’ said Stars, ‘it is a new ghost! A grandmotherly ghost! Perhaps she will darn our socks for us.’

‘Better yet,’ replied Stripes, ‘perhaps we can teach her to play poker. Bezique is so frightfully dull.’

One evening, as she was dressing for dinner, a faint, shimmering figure appeared in her looking-glass. It was the apparition of an elderly lady, dressed in the severe black silk of the early Victorian era, her hair pulled into a tight bun. She had a long, disapproving nose and a mouth set in a firm line.

‘You are the new mistress of this house,’ the ghost said, her voice a dry rustle, like old leaves. ‘I am Lady Augusta de Canterville. I have been in residence since 1853. I must insist that you do something about the lighting. It is garishly bright and entirely unbecoming.’

Virginia, who had faced down the terrifying Sir Simon, was not to be intimidated by a lecture on interior decoration. ‘I am the Duchess of Cheshire,’ she said calmly. ‘And we find the electric lights very convenient.’

The ghost of Lady Augusta looked aghast. ‘Convenience,’ she sniffed, ‘is the mother of vulgarity. In my day, we valued atmosphere. And another thing; that French cook must go. Peppermint has a cleansing, clarifying effect on the palate. She has no appreciation for it.’

Lady Augusta would spend the night rearranging the furniture according to her own severe aesthetic, and the servants would spend the morning putting it back. She would chill the wine that was meant to be served at room temperature and warm the champagne. She left critical, spectral notes on the menus, suggesting more gruel and less sauce. It was to be a triumph of modern hospitality.

As the guests began to arrive, a bitter, unnatural cold descended upon the ballroom. The flowers wilted in their vases. A ghostly mist, smelling faintly of disapproval and mothballs, began to rise from the floorboards.

The guests shivered and looked around in confusion. The Duchess’s great-aunt, a formidable dowager, was heard to remark that the chill was even worse than at Balmoral in November.

The Duke, seeing his wife’s beautiful party on the verge of ruin, was about to make a firm speech to the empty air, but Virginia stopped him. She had a better idea. Walking to the centre of the ballroom, her voice ringing out with a clear and gentle authority, she addressed the invisible presence.

‘Lady Augusta,’ she said, ‘I know you mean well. I know you wish for this house to be run with decorum and grace. And for that, I thank you.’

The chill in the air lessened slightly. The mist seemed to pause in its swirling.

‘But you see,’ Virginia continued, ‘times have changed. These are our friends. This is how we show our joy. We cannot live in the past, no matter how elegant it may have been. But that does not mean we must forget it. Your taste and your knowledge are a part of this house’s history. A history we cherish.’

She turned to the orchestra leader. ‘A waltz, if you please,’ she commanded. ‘A waltz for Lady Augusta.’

The musicians, recovering their composure, struck up a beautiful, old-fashioned melody. Virginia turned to her husband. ‘Cecil,’ she said, ‘I believe Lady Augusta would like to dance.’

The Duke, for all his levity, understood his wife perfectly. He bowed deeply to the empty space before him. ‘Lady Augusta,’ he said with the utmost gravity, ‘may I have the honour?’

He held out his arms, and to the astonishment of all present, he began to waltz, quite gracefully, with an invisible partner. He spun and he turned, guided by a force no one could see. A warm breeze swept through the ballroom, and the mist dissolved. The flowers seemed to perk up in their vases, and the lights shone with a soft, golden radiance. As the Duke twirled his unseen partner past the great windows, several guests swore they saw a faint, shimmering reflection in the glass: a stern old lady, held in the arms of a handsome young man, a look of profound and surprised delight on her spectral face.

When the music ended, the Duke bowed again. The air was still, and the presence was gone. The party, saved from the brink of disaster, went on to be the most talked-about event of the season.

Lady Augusta was never so disruptive again. She did not leave; rather, she seemed to come to an understanding. The occasional lace handkerchief would still appear, and sometimes a piece of furniture would be nudged a few inches to the left, but these were no longer acts of protest. They were suggestions, offered from one mistress of Canterville to another. Virginia, for her part, would sometimes leave a cup of weak, peppermint tea in the Blue Bedchamber before retiring, a small gesture of respect across the centuries.

One evening, months later, the Duke found his wife looking thoughtfully into the fire. ‘It is a curious thing,’ he said, taking her hand. ‘Sir Simon needed tears and prayers to find his peace. Lady Eleanore needed a frightfully vulgar business plan. What was it, do you suppose, that our dear Lady Augusta needed?’

Virginia smiled and leaned her head on his shoulder. She had learned from Sir Simon that Love was stronger than Death. She had learned from Lady Eleanore that Commerce was stronger than Pride. And from Lady Augusta, she had learned a lesson perhaps most useful of all for the mistress of a great house.

‘Respect,’ she said softly. ‘And a really good waltz.’

Washington had married a celebrated English beauty with a fortune even larger than his own, and had devoted himself to collecting rare books and cultivating an impressive collection of orchids. Mr. and Mrs. Otis, finding the English climate disagreed with them in the long run, eventually returned to America, leaving the Chase in the capable hands of their daughter and son-in-law. The ghosts, it seemed, were gone for good, and the only spirits to be found in the house were those poured into glasses at dinnertime.

It was this very peace that began to trouble the new Duke of Cheshire, who, despite his title and his newfound responsibilities, had never quite lost the mischievous spirit of his boyhood. ‘It is all very well, you know,’ he remarked one evening to Virginia, as they sat in the Great Hall, which was now brightly lit by electric lamps of Mr. Otis’s own design. ‘But the place has become dreadfully respectable. One almost misses the rattling chains and the spectral laughter.’

‘Cecil, don’t be absurd,’ said Virginia, though she smiled as she said it. ‘Poor Sir Simon earned his rest. And think of the servants; Cook was threatening to leave every other week.’

‘I know, I know,’ he sighed, ‘but it was an adventure. Now all we have to look forward to are county fairs and visits from my great-aunt. And she is far more terrifying than Sir Simon ever was, I can tell you.’

It was as if some unseen power had been listening to the Duke’s idle complaint, for it was not a week later that the first signs of a new and altogether different sort of disturbance began. It did not start with a blood-stain or a groan, but with a subtle and pervasive scent of potpourri, of a kind that had not been fashionable for at least fifty years, that seemed to emanate from the Queen Anne suite. Then, the Blue Bedchamber, a room notorious for its dampness, suddenly became the warmest and driest room in the house, its curtains perpetually drawn against the midday sun. Small, neatly folded lace handkerchiefs began to appear on pillows, and a ghostly game of bezique seemed to be in progress in the drawing-room, for the cards would be found rearranged every morning into inexplicable hands.

The staff were the first to notice the full extent of the problem. A footman complained that an invisible hand kept straightening his cravat. A housemaid gave notice after finding her carefully made bed had been unmade and remade with hospital corners and a lavender sachet tucked under the pillow. The cook, a formidable Frenchwoman, flew into a rage when she discovered that her boeuf bourguignon had been mysteriously seasoned with a large quantity of peppermint, a flavour she abhorred with a deep and professional passion.

Washington, on a visit from his own country estate, was fascinated. ‘It is a most curious phenomenon,’ he declared, taking copious notes. ‘These are not the actions of a malevolent or tortured spirit, like Sir Simon. The manifestations are benign, almost… fussy. It is a domestic haunting. A haunting of tidiness.’

The twins, who had come down for the weekend, were delighted. ‘I say, Stripes,’ said Stars, ‘it is a new ghost! A grandmotherly ghost! Perhaps she will darn our socks for us.’

‘Better yet,’ replied Stripes, ‘perhaps we can teach her to play poker. Bezique is so frightfully dull.’

It was Virginia who felt the true nature of the presence. It was a gentle spirit, she sensed, but a lonely one, and one possessed of a will of iron. One evening, as she was dressing for dinner, a faint, shimmering figure appeared in her looking-glass. It was the apparition of an elderly lady, dressed in the severe black silk of the early Victorian era, her hair pulled into a tight bun. She had a long, disapproving nose and a mouth set in a firm line.

‘You are the new mistress of this house,’ the ghost said, her voice a dry rustle, like old leaves. ‘I am Lady Augusta de Canterville. I have been in residence since 1853. I must insist that you do something about the lighting. It is garishly bright and entirely unbecoming.’

Virginia, who had faced down the terrifying Sir Simon, was not to be intimidated by a lecture on interior decoration. ‘I am the Duchess of Cheshire,’ she said calmly. ‘And we find the electric lights very convenient.’

The ghost of Lady Augusta looked aghast. ‘Convenience,’ she sniffed, ‘is the mother of vulgarity. In my day, we valued atmosphere. And another thing; that French cook must go. Peppermint has a cleansing, clarifying effect on the palate. She has no appreciation for it.’

This, Virginia realised, was a haunting of a different order. Sir Simon had wanted to inspire terror; Lady Augusta wanted to manage the household.

Over the next few weeks, a strange war was waged at Canterville Chase. It was a war of taste. Lady Augusta would spend the night rearranging the furniture according to her own severe aesthetic, and the servants would spend the morning putting it back. She would chill the wine that was meant to be served at room temperature and warm the champagne. She left critical, spectral notes on the menus, suggesting more gruel and less sauce. She took a particular dislike to the Duke’s collection of modern art, which she would turn to face the wall every night.

The Duke found it all immensely amusing. ‘It is like having my mother-in-law here, but without the expense of feeding her,’ he laughed.

But Virginia saw the loneliness behind the criticism. ‘She simply does not understand,’ she told her husband. ‘The world has changed, and she is left behind, trying to keep things as they were.’

The crisis came to a head at the annual Canterville summer ball. It was the highlight of the local social calendar, and Virginia had spent weeks planning it. The house was filled with flowers, a string orchestra was brought in from London, and the new electric lamps were festooned with coloured paper lanterns. It was to be a triumph of modern hospitality.

Lady Augusta was horrified. The noise, the lights, the sheer number of people; it was an affront to every principle of genteel living she held dear. As the guests began to arrive, a bitter, unnatural cold descended upon the ballroom. The flowers wilted in their vases. The violins produced a series of excruciating screeches, as if their strings were being tightened by an unseen and unmusical hand. A ghostly mist, smelling faintly of disapproval and mothballs, began to rise from the floorboards.

The guests shivered and looked around in confusion. The Duchess’s great-aunt, a formidable dowager, was heard to remark that the chill was even worse than at Balmoral in November.

The Duke, seeing his wife’s beautiful party on the verge of ruin, was about to make a firm speech to the empty air, but Virginia stopped him. She had a better idea. Walking to the centre of the ballroom, her voice ringing out with a clear and gentle authority, she addressed the invisible presence.

‘Lady Augusta,’ she said, ‘I know you mean well. I know you wish for this house to be run with decorum and grace. And for that, I thank you.’

The chill in the air lessened slightly. The mist seemed to pause in its swirling.

‘But you see,’ Virginia continued, ‘times have changed. These are our friends. This is how we show our joy. We cannot live in the past, no matter how elegant it may have been. But that does not mean we must forget it. Your taste and your knowledge are a part of this house’s history. A history we cherish.’

She turned to the orchestra leader. ‘A waltz, if you please,’ she commanded. ‘A waltz for Lady Augusta.’

The musicians, recovering their composure, struck up a beautiful, old-fashioned melody. Virginia turned to her husband. ‘Cecil,’ she said, ‘I believe Lady Augusta would like to dance.’

The Duke, for all his levity, understood his wife perfectly. He bowed deeply to the empty space before him. ‘Lady Augusta,’ he said with the utmost gravity, ‘may I have the honour?’

He held out his arms, and to the astonishment of all present, he began to waltz, quite gracefully, with an invisible partner. He spun and he turned, guided by a force no one could see. A warm breeze swept through the ballroom, and the mist dissolved. The flowers seemed to perk up in their vases, and the lights shone with a soft, golden radiance. As the Duke twirled his unseen partner past the great windows, several guests swore they saw a faint, shimmering reflection in the glass: a stern old lady, held in the arms of a handsome young man, a look of profound and surprised delight on her spectral face.

When the music ended, the Duke bowed again. The air was still, and the presence was gone. The party, saved from the brink of disaster, went on to be the most talked-about event of the season.

Lady Augusta was never so disruptive again. She did not leave; rather, she seemed to come to an understanding. The occasional lace handkerchief would still appear, and sometimes a piece of furniture would be nudged a few inches to the left, but these were no longer acts of protest. They were suggestions, offered from one mistress of Canterville to another. Virginia, for her part, would sometimes leave a cup of weak, peppermint tea in the Blue Bedchamber before retiring, a small gesture of respect across the centuries.

One evening, months later, the Duke found his wife looking thoughtfully into the fire. ‘It is a curious thing,’ he said, taking her hand. ‘Sir Simon needed tears and prayers to find his peace. Lady Eleanore needed a frightfully vulgar business plan. What was it, do you suppose, that our dear Lady Augusta needed?’

Virginia smiled and leaned her head on his shoulder. She had learned from Sir Simon that Love was stronger than Death. She had learned from Lady Eleanore that Commerce was stronger than Pride. And from Lady Augusta, she had learned a lesson perhaps most useful of all for the mistress of a great house.

‘Respect,’ she said softly. ‘And a really good waltz.’

When they went up to bed, they found Virginia waiting for them on the landing. A faint smile was on her parted lips, and she held a small, withered sprig of peppermint in her hand. ‘It is for Lady Augusta,’ she said quietly. ‘I think she will like the scent.’ Then she kissed her father and mother, wished the boys a cheerful good-night, and went to her own room, leaving the Duke to follow her with a look of such profound adoration that the twins were obliged to beat a hasty retreat to their own quarters to keep from bursting into unseemly laughter. And so, a great and profound peace settled over Canterville Chase. The ghosts, it seemed, had been thoroughly and systematically pacified, one by a funeral, one by a merger, and one, it appeared, by a waltz. The house took on an air of almost disappointing normality. Mrs. Otis’s prize-winning roses bloomed unmolested, Mr. Otis’s patented stain remover was retired to a high shelf in the pantry, and the twins, for want of any supernatural mischief, were forced to turn their considerable talents for disruption upon the local village, a development for which the rural policeman was not at all grateful. The seasons turned, and the family grew even more fond of their ancient home. Washington Otis, who had become something of an authority on the history of the Canterville family, spent his days cataloguing the library and his evenings writing long, scholarly letters to the British Museum. He had, he confessed to Virginia, found his true calling not in diplomacy or commerce, but in the quiet, dusty world of historical footnotes, a revelation that surprised no one at all. It was on a late autumn evening, when a wild wind was howling round the old house and the rain was beating against the mullioned windows, that the first hint of a new disturbance made itself known. The family was gathered in the library, enjoying the cheerful blaze of the fire. Mr. Otis was reading a rather dry pamphlet on modern agricultural drainage, Mrs. Otis was embroidering a set of doilies with the family crest, an enterprise she considered the very height of aristocratic elegance, and the Duke was attempting to teach a small and very unwilling terrier to balance a biscuit on its nose. Suddenly, above the roar of the storm, another sound was heard. It was faint at first, a distant, mournful cry that seemed to be carried on the wind, followed by a faint baying, like a pack of hounds very far away. ‘Good heavens,’ said Mrs. Otis, looking up from her embroidery with a nervous start, ‘what was that dreadful noise?’ ‘Poachers, I expect,’ said Mr. Otis, without looking up from his pamphlet. ‘I’ve told the gamekeeper to be more vigilant. A disgraceful disturbance of the peace.’ The little Duke, however, had gone rather pale. ‘It sounded,’ he said, in a low voice, ‘like a hunting horn.’ Virginia, who had been sitting quietly in the shadows, felt a curious chill creep over her, a chill that had nothing to do with the autumn night. The sound was not heard again, and the incident was soon forgotten, but a week later, it returned. This time the night was clear and still, with a great, white moon hanging in the sky like a silver dish. The family had just retired for the night when the horn blew again, much closer this time, a single, sharp, imperious blast that echoed across the park. It was followed almost immediately by the frantic yelping of hounds and the thunder of what sounded like a dozen horses galloping at full tilt across the manicured lawns. The twins were the first to the window, their faces pressed against the cold glass. ‘There’s nothing there!’ they cried in unison, their voices a mixture of disappointment and excitement. ‘Absolutely nothing!’ Mr. Otis appeared in his dressing-gown, holding a candle in one hand and a revolver in the other, a habit he had acquired during his early political career and had never quite abandoned. He strode to the window and peered out into the moonlit darkness. The lawn was indeed empty, its smooth, green surface unblemished, save for a few fallen leaves. Yet the sounds of the invisible hunt were unmistakable now: the crash of unseen bodies through the shrubbery, the snapping of twigs, and the wild, triumphant cries of a huntsman urging on his pack. ‘This is an outrage!’ declared Mr. Otis, his practical American mind deeply offended by a phenomenon that could trample his property without even having the decency to exist. ‘It is trespassing of the most egregious kind. Tomorrow I shall have signs posted. I will not have spectral equestrians ruining the turf.’ The strange occurrences continued for several weeks. The ghostly hunt, for that is what everyone now called it, would appear without warning on moonlit nights, its phantom noises a source of constant agitation for Mrs. Otis and a subject of intense scientific interest for the twins, who spent a great deal of time and energy trying to capture the baying of the hounds in a phonograph, with a singular lack of success. It was Washington, however, who made the first real breakthrough. He had been spending his days poring over a dusty, leather-bound volume he had discovered in a locked cabinet, entitled ‘Curious Legends and Sorrows of the House of Canterville’. Late one evening, he came into the drawing-room with a triumphant look on his face, a look he usually reserved for the discovery of a particularly rare postage stamp. ‘I have found him,’ he announced, placing the heavy book on the table. ‘I know who our huntsman is.’ He pointed to a chapter illustrated with a rather gruesome woodcut of a man on a black horse, surrounded by demonic-looking dogs. ‘Allow me to introduce you to Lord Geoffrey de Canterville, known to his contemporaries as ‘The Black Huntsman’. He was, by all accounts, a thoroughly unpleasant fellow. He lived in the fourteenth century and was famous for two things: his passion for the chase and his spectacular cruelty. He hunted everything, you see, man and beast, with equal relish. His end came on All Hallows’ Eve in 1374. The story goes that he was pursuing a magnificent white stag, and in his frenzy, he and his hounds galloped straight into the consecrated ground of the local priory, trampling the Abbot, who had tried to stand in his way.’ ‘How perfectly dreadful!’ exclaimed Mrs. Otis. ‘Indeed,’ Washington continued, warming to his subject. ‘His punishment was divine, or at least, infernally poetic. He is cursed to ride forever, eternally hunting a quarry he can never catch. His hunt is a re-enactment of his own damnation. They call it the ‘Wild Chase’, and it is said to bring ruin and despair to any who witness it.’ ‘Ruin my prize petunias, more like,’ muttered Mr. Otis. ‘Is there any mention of how to stop this nuisance?’ Washington turned a page. ‘There is a fragment of an old ballad, though the meaning is rather obscure. It says: When the Hart that runs for aye Finds its rest at break of day, When the Hunter’s horn is broken, By a jest that is not spoken, Then the Chase shall lose its fire And the Hunter’s rage expire.’ Virginia, who had been listening intently, repeated the lines softly to herself. ‘A jest that is not spoken,’ she murmured. ‘What can that possibly mean?’ No one had an answer, and for the next few days, a sense of gloom descended upon the house. The Wild Chase grew bolder. One night the ghostly hounds were heard scrabbling at the very doors of the house, and the terrified cook swore she saw a pair of glowing red eyes peering in at her through the kitchen window. The little Duke of Cheshire, who had come to stay, spent his nights patrolling the corridors with an antique blunderbuss, determined to protect Virginia from the spectral menace, a gesture which she found both touching and entirely absurd. It was the twins who decided to take matters into their own hands. Having failed to capture the ghosts with technology, they decided to resort to their own unique brand of practical magic. That night, they waited with bated breath. The horn blew, the hounds bayed, the phantom hooves thundered down the avenue, and then, there was a series of spectral splashes, silent thuds, and what the twins later described as a "ghostly poof". For a moment, there was a stunned silence, and then, a roar of incandescent, otherworldly fury that shook the very foundations of the house. The invisible Lord Geoffrey, it seemed, did not appreciate being doused in phantom flour and feathers. The hunt, more frenzied than ever, tore through the gardens, uprooting a whole row of young cypress trees Mr. Otis had just had planted, and vanished with a final, furious blast of the horn. ‘Well,’ said Mr. Otis the next morning, surveying the damage with a grim expression, ‘that plan was an unmitigated failure. She had been quiet and thoughtful all morning, but now her eyes shone with that strange, determined light they had all come to recognise. ‘I think I know what we must do,’ she said. ‘Washington, the ballad said the hunter’s horn must be broken by a jest that is not spoken. The twins tried to play a trick on him, and it only made him angrier. I think that is because their jest was spoken, in a way. It was a direct challenge. We have been trying to fight him, or trick him, or ignore him.’ She turned to her father. ‘You have all been treating him as a serious problem. A nuisance, a menace, a historical curiosity. But what if the way to defeat him is to refuse to take him seriously at all?’ ‘My dear,’ said Mrs. Otis, ‘the ghost of a fourteenth-century murderer is a very serious thing indeed.’ ‘Is it?’ asked Virginia. ‘He has been raging for five hundred years because of one terrible mistake. He is trapped in his own anger. Perhaps what he needs, more than anything else, is to be reminded of how ridiculous he has become.’ A plan was formed, a plan so audacious, so utterly American in its cheerful disregard for history and decorum, that only the Otis family could have conceived of it. That evening, as the moon rose, they did not hide in the house. Instead, they prepared for their own hunt. Mr. Otis put on his riding boots and stood on the front steps, holding not a whip, but a large, brass megaphone and a legal pad. Washington brought out a telescope, which he set up on a tripod, as if observing a celestial event. Mrs. Otis arranged a set of chairs on the lawn and prepared a large thermos of hot chocolate, as though settling in for a fireworks display. The little Duke, at Virginia’s request, saddled his pony, but armed himself only with a bag of sugar lumps. The twins, dressed in their brightest plaid knickerbockers, were given bicycle bells and party horns. At last, as the clock struck midnight, the dreaded sound was heard. The mournful horn, the baying hounds, the thunder of hooves. Out of the mists at the end of the avenue, the Wild Chase appeared, more terrifying than ever before. A great black horse with eyes of fire, carrying a rider cloaked in shadow, surrounded by a pack of slavering, spectral hounds. They charged towards the house, expecting fear, and terror, and a cowering populace. What they found was the Otis family. As the ghostly cavalcade bore down on him, Mr. Otis raised his megaphone. ‘Attention!’ he boomed, his voice echoing unnaturally in the night air. ‘You are in violation of County Ordinance 7, subsection C, regarding nocturnal disturbances! I am issuing a formal citation for excessive noise, property damage, and failure to yield to a properly constituted household!’ The Black Huntsman faltered, his horse taking a hesitant step. This was not the reaction he was accustomed to. At that moment, the twins shot past on their bicycles, ringing their bells and tooting their party horns with wild abandon. ‘Tally-ho!’ they shouted, attempting to herd the spectral hounds, who looked utterly baffled by the small, fast-moving creatures weaving between their legs. Washington, peering through his telescope, made loud, academic pronouncements. ‘Fascinating! The ectoplasmic-to-kinetic energy conversion is remarkably inefficient! I estimate a thermal loss of at least forty per cent!’ The Duke of Cheshire trotted forward on his pony, holding out a sugar lump. ‘There, there, old chap,’ he said soothingly to the great, fiery-eyed demon steed. ‘Had a long night, have you? How about a treat?’ The horse, which had been breathing spectral fire only moments before, stopped dead and snorted in what could only be described as profound confusion. The entire hunt ground to a halt. The hounds ceased their baying and began to sniff uncertainly at the bicycle tires. The Black Huntsman, Lord Geoffrey de Canterville, sat motionless on his horse, a figure of impotent rage. His curse was built on a foundation of terror, his power derived from the fear he inspired. But these people were not afraid. They were not even respectful. They were treating his eternal, gothic damnation as a sort of quaint, provincial pageant. He had been met with violence and prayer and magic for five hundred years, but he had never, in all his haunting, been met with such cheerful, organised, and overwhelming absurdity. He raised his horn to his lips to blow a blast of pure fury, to reassert his terrifying authority, but no sound came out. He looked down at the scene: at the man with the megaphone, the boy with the telescope, the lady with the hot chocolate, the two small demons on their wheeled contraptions, and the ridiculous young fop trying to feed his hell-horse a lump of sugar. And then his gaze fell upon Virginia. She was standing a little apart from the others, not laughing, not participating in the chaos. She was simply watching him, and in her eyes there was no fear at all, only a deep and overwhelming pity. It was the final, crushing blow. A look of utter bewilderment crossed his shadowy features. He looked at his horn, then at the ridiculous scene before him, and then back at the girl. For the first time in five centuries, the rage began to cool. The fire in his eyes flickered and died. The jest had not been spoken; it had been lived. The sheer, glorious, undignified farce of it all had broken him. With a sound like a long, weary sigh, he and his horse and his hounds began to fade. They did not vanish in a crash of thunder, but simply dissolved into the moonlit air, like smoke from an extinguished candle. The horn fell from his grasp and clattered onto the lawn, becoming, for a single instant, a solid piece of blackened metal before it, too, crumbled into dust. A profound silence fell over Canterville Chase, a silence deeper and more peaceful than any it had known before. Mr. Otis lowered his megaphone. ‘Well,’ he said, with immense satisfaction. ‘I believe that settles the matter.’ In the hall, as they drank Mrs. Otis’s hot chocolate, the Duke turned to Virginia. ‘You were right, as you always are,’ he said. ‘But I confess I still do not quite understand. What finally vanquished him?’ Virginia smiled, a gentle, knowing smile that made her look far older than her years. She had seen the despair in Sir Simon, the pride in Lady Eleanore, the loneliness in Lady Augusta. In the Black Huntsman, she had seen five hundred years of pointless, self-perpetuating anger. ‘He wasn’t defeated,’ she said softly. ‘He was embarrassed. I suppose even a terrible curse cannot long survive being made to feel utterly and completely ridiculous.’ And with that, the last ghost of Canterville was laid to rest, not with tears or prayers, but with the invincible power of a jest, and the unshakeable, and at times quite baffling, sanity of the Otis family.

It is designed to detect and locate spectral energy signatures.’

Mr. Otis stared at the contraption. ‘And what, in layman’s terms, is that supposed to do?’

‘It finds ghosts, Papa,’ said Stars simply. ‘And where there is a ghost, we may find Virginia. We believe she has been taken into another plane of existence. The Indicator’s needle will point to the epicentre of the disturbance. We have only to follow it.’

Washington looked as if he wanted to confiscate the device, but the little Duke, his eyes gleaming with a sudden new hope, rushed over to the twins. ‘By Jove, that’s brilliant!’ he exclaimed. ‘A ghost-finder! Let us try it at once! Why did you not say so before?’

‘The prototype was not fully calibrated,’ said Stripes, making a minute adjustment to one of the dials. ‘We had to cross-reference the atmospheric density with the half-life of a standard phantasm. It is a delicate process.’

The twins led the way, holding their Ectoplasmic Resonance Indicator with the gravity of priests carrying a sacred relic. ‘Trouble!’ cried the Duke, rushing forward and taking her hand, which felt as cold as marble. ‘My dearest Virginia, we thought we had lost you forever! Your hand is freezing! You must come to the fire at once.’

Mr. Otis, who had recovered his composure more quickly than the others, stepped forward, his expression a mixture of relief and intense curiosity. ‘Virginia,’ he said, in his most businesslike tone, ‘I demand an explanation. Where have you been for the last five hours?’

Virginia looked at her father, a small, sad smile playing on her lips. ‘I have been with the Ghost,’ she said simply.

A collective gasp went through the room. Mrs. Otis immediately fell back onto the sofa and called for her smelling salts.

‘The Ghost?’ repeated Mr. Otis, raising an eyebrow. ‘You mean to tell me that this entire uproar, which has involved the local constabulary, a troop of innocent gypsies, and a frantic Duke, was caused by Sir Simon?’

‘He did not mean for it to happen,’ said Virginia quietly. ‘He needed my help. There was a prophecy, you see, on the library window.’

‘The one about the golden girl and the barren almond?’ asked Washington, who had a great fondness for anything that smacked of the romantic.

‘Yes,’ said Virginia. ‘I had to weep for him, because he had no tears, and pray for him, because he had no faith. I went with him to the Garden of Death.’

The little Duke shuddered. ‘The Garden of Death! Virginia, what are you saying? It sounds perfectly dreadful!’

‘No,’ she said, her eyes looking far away, as if seeing something none of them could. ‘It was not dreadful at all. It was very peaceful. He is at rest now. The Angel of Death has had mercy on him.’

She walked over to the window and drew back the heavy curtain. Outside, in the moonlight, they could all see the great almond-tree that grew by the lawn. It was covered in a sudden and glorious profusion of white blossoms, as if it had been touched by a miracle.

‘The barren almond bears,’ she whispered. ‘It is all over. The house is still. Peace has come to Canterville.’

There was a long silence after this, broken only by the crackling of the fire. The Otis family, being eminently practical people, did not quite know what to make of a story that involved prophecies and Angels of Death. Mr. Otis was the first to speak.

‘Well,’ he said, clearing his throat, ‘it appears we owe the gypsies an apology and a rather generous gratuity. And I suppose I must send another set of telegrams to recall the first set. It is all most irregular.’ He looked at his daughter, whose face was illuminated by the moonlight, and a flicker of understanding, or perhaps just paternal pride, crossed his face. ‘In any case,’ he concluded, ‘we are glad to have you back, Virginia.’

And so, the strange adventure of the Otis family and the Canterville Ghost came to a close. Virginia, however, found that her own adventure had only just begun. She had walked in the domain of shadows, and it had left an indelible mark upon her soul. While she resumed her life, she was not quite the same girl who had entered the Tapestry Chamber. There was a new gravity in her eyes, a serenity in her demeanour that puzzled and, at times, worried her young husband, the Duke of Cheshire.

After their honeymoon, a grand tour of the continent which Cecil had planned with meticulous, boyish enthusiasm, they returned to England and settled into the rhythm of London society. The Duke, who adored his young wife, showered her with all the attentions and luxuries he could imagine. He bought her emeralds to match her eyes, and thoroughbred horses for riding in the park, and filled their Mayfair house with the gayest and most fashionable people in London. Virginia accepted it all with a gentle grace, but Cecil could not help but notice a certain reserve, a quiet melancholy that he could not penetrate.

She would often sit for long periods, staring out of a window, her hands lying still in her lap, and he would ask her what she was thinking. ‘Oh, nothing, Cecil,’ she would say, her smile not quite reaching her eyes. ‘Just about things.’

This was not an answer that satisfied the Duke in the slightest. He was a man of action and simple, cheerful pleasures, and ‘things’ was a category altogether too vague and troubling for his comfort. He began to fear she was not happy.

‘Is it me, Virginia?’ he asked one evening, his handsome face creased with worry. ‘Have I done something to displease you? Is married life not what you expected?’

‘No, of course not, Cecil,’ she said, taking his hand. ‘You are the kindest and best of husbands. It is only… I learned something, that night at Canterville. Something that has changed the way I see the world.’

‘The ghost, you mean,’ he said, a note of impatience in his voice. ‘My darling, it is over. The poor fellow is at peace. You must try to forget it. Life is for the living!’

‘But that is just it, Cecil,’ she replied softly. ‘He taught me what Life is.’

The matter came to a head some months later, when the Duke’s grandmother, the Dowager Duchess of Dumbleton, a formidable old lady with a face like a hawk and a reputation for a terrifyingly sharp tongue, announced her intention to host a grand ball in their honour. The crowning event of the evening, she had declared, was to be the first public appearance of the new Duchess of Cheshire wearing the famous Canterville jewels.

Cecil, delighted at the prospect, had the sandalwood box brought from the vault. He opened it himself, and the diamonds flashed and glittered under the gaslight, a river of captured stars.

‘There!’ he said, with a triumphant smile. ‘Are they not magnificent? All of London will be mad with jealousy.’

Virginia looked at the necklace, and a shadow passed over her face. ‘I cannot wear them, Cecil,’ she said.

The Duke stared at her in astonishment. ‘Cannot wear them? But why ever not? They are your wedding gift! They are beyond compare!’

‘They were his,’ she said, her voice barely a whisper. ‘They belong to his memory. To wear them to a ball… it would feel like a betrayal. He suffered so much, Cecil.’

‘He was a murderer!’ the Duke retorted, his patience finally snapping. ‘He murdered his wife, and by all accounts he was a dreadful nuisance for three hundred years! He was a sinner, Virginia, by his own admission! To be frank, I think he got off rather lightly!’

‘You do not understand,’ she said, and turned away, her shoulders trembling.

The Duke was instantly remorseful. He went to her and put his arms around her. ‘Forgive me, my love,’ he murmured. ‘I am a brute. Of course you need not wear them if it pains you. We shall say they are being reset. My grandmother will be furious, but I can handle her. I only want you to be happy.’

It was Mr. Otis who, in his own practical way, provided the beginning of a solution. He had written to them from America, having decided, after much deliberation, to sell Canterville Chase. The house, he wrote, had served its purpose. Its ghost was gone, its curse was lifted, and it was altogether too large and draughty for a modern family. An offer had been made by a Lord Warburton, a noted collector of historical properties, and Mr. Otis was inclined to accept.

When Virginia read the letter, she felt a pang of such acute loss that it surprised her. The thought of Lord Warburton, a man known for his cold cynicism and his habit of turning old estates into private museums, taking possession of the Chase was unbearable. Canterville was not a museum; it was a place of suffering and redemption. It was where a soul had been saved.

She showed the letter to Cecil, who read it with a thoughtful frown. ‘Warburton,’ he said. ‘A dreadful fellow. He came to my club last week and held forth for an hour on what he called “the foolish mythologies of the landed gentry.” He believes the Canterville ghost was a hoax perpetrated by your family to increase the property’s value before selling it.’

Virginia’s eyes flashed with a fire Cecil had not seen since she had stood up to the ghost himself. ‘He said that?’

‘I am afraid so. He is a man with no poetry in his soul. He plans, I hear, to remove the bloodstain with a new chemical process and to brick up the wall in the Tapestry Chamber.’

That evening, Virginia was very quiet during dinner. Cecil watched her, his heart aching with a familiar sense of helplessness. But later, as they sat in their drawing-room, she came and stood before him, her face pale but resolute.

‘Cecil,’ she said, ‘there is something I must ask of you. It is a great deal, I know.’

‘Anything, my love,’ he said, taking her hands.

‘Do not let my father sell the Chase to Lord Warburton. Let us buy it ourselves.’

The Duke was taken aback. ‘Buy Canterville? But my darling, what would we do with it? It is miles from anywhere, and as your father says, it is dreadfully draughty. We have three of our own country estates already.’

‘I do not wish to live there,’ Virginia said. ‘I wish to preserve it. It is a special place. A sacred place, in its own way. Sir Simon’s grave is in the churchyard. The almond tree blossoms for him. It is a place where a great secret was revealed. We cannot let it fall into the hands of a man who would mock it, who would scrub away its history with chemicals.’ She looked at him, her eyes pleading. ‘He taught me about love, Cecil. The kind of love that is stronger than death. I feel I owe him this. To protect his memory, and the peace he finally found.’

Cecil looked at his wife, and for the first time, he began to see. He saw not a melancholic girl pining over a morbid fantasy, but a woman of profound conviction and loyalty. He saw that her experience with the ghost had not broken her, but had instead forged her into something finer, deeper, and more wonderful than the girl he had fallen in love with. The ‘sadness’ he had feared was not sadness at all; it was wisdom.

He stood up and, with a gravity that befEtted his title, he kissed her forehead. ‘You are right,’ he said. ‘It is the only thing to be do. I shall write to your father in the morning. And I shall have my solicitor inform Lord Warburton that Canterville Chase is no longer on the market.’

A brilliant smile, the first truly radiant smile he had seen in months, broke across Virginia’s face. ‘Oh, Cecil!’ she cried, throwing her arms around his neck. ‘I knew you would understand!’

‘I am beginning to,’ he said, holding her tightly. ‘I am beginning to understand that I have married not just a golden girl, but a woman of uncommon strength and spirit.’ He paused, and then added with a twinkle in his eye, ‘And I must confess, the thought of thwarting that dreadful fellow Warburton gives me the most enormous satisfaction.’

From that day forward, a new understanding blossomed between them, as miraculous in its own way as the almond tree at Canterville. Cecil never again asked her to wear the Canterville jewels, and they remained in their sandalwood box, not as a source of contention, but as a shared symbol of a past they both agreed to honour. They purchased the Chase from Mr. Otis, who was delighted to keep the property in the family, and they established a small endowment to ensure its upkeep, and to tend to the churchyard where Sir Simon de Canterville lay at peace under a simple stone.

They did not visit often, but on the anniversary of that strange night, Virginia would sometimes make the journey. She would walk through the quiet rooms, and stand before the prophecy on the library window, and look at the tapestry of the little huntsmen who had tried to warn her away. She would feel not sadness, but a deep and abiding gratitude. The house was no longer haunted by a troubled spirit; instead, it seemed to be filled with a profound and lasting peace, the echo of a prayer answered, and a sinner forgiven. It was a testament not to death, but to the enduring power of a little girl’s pity, and the extraordinary strength of a love that had dared to walk into the darkness and lead a lost soul into the light.

It was not a diary of daily events, but a series of poems and meditations, the outpourings of a soul in deep and inconsolable pain. It was the voice of Lady Eleanor de Canterville.

She wrote not of a cruel husband, but of a man she adored with a desperate, all-consuming passion. But she also wrote of a ‘shadow in the mind,’ a ‘leaden grief’ that had settled upon her at birth and would not be lifted. She described the world as a grey and tuneless place, and life as a cage from which she longed to be free. The birth of her children had brought not joy, but a deeper terror, a fear that she would pass her shadow on to them.

‘My Simon pleads with me to live,’ Virginia read, her own eyes filling with tears. ‘He brings me jesters from the court, and nightingales in silver cages, and says my smile is all the sun he needs. The room was utterly still, the only sound Virginia’s soft, sad voice. She turned a few more pages, her fingers gentle on the brittle paper.

‘He has finally understood,’ she read on. ‘My beloved, my heart, my Simon. He weeps, for he does not wish to be my gaoler in this life any longer. He has read the poets who say that love is stronger than death, and he believes he can love me even there. Tonight, when the moon is hidden, he will give me the gift I have so long begged him for. He will open the door for me. It is not a sin, he says, but an act of the most profound and terrible love. He will unlock my cage and let the tired bird fly free. Virginia looked up, her face a mask of stunned revelation. ‘He didn’t murder her,’ she whispered. ‘He helped her. It was… a mercy.’

She read the final entry, dated only a day later. The script was ragged, almost illegible. ‘Her brothers have come. They do not understand love; they understand only property and honour.
