The book fell from Virginia’s fingers onto her lap. The secret of Canterville Chase was not a simple, brutal murder, but a tragedy of love and despair so deep it had echoed for three hundred years. Sir Simon’s sin was not just the taking of a life, but the terrible, loving choice that had damned him, a choice for which he could find no forgiveness until a little girl had wept for him, not knowing the true depth of what she was weeping for.

No one spoke. Even the twins were pale and subdued. The silence was finally broken by Mr. Hiram B. Otis. He took off his spectacles and wiped them, though there was no dust upon them. He looked at the little book, at the dried flower, and then at his daughter, whose face was illuminated by a kind of sorrowful wisdom.

‘Virginia,’ he said, and his voice was thick with an emotion she had never heard in it before. ‘My dear girl. You were right.’ He walked over to the great fireplace and took the bundle of architectural plans and financial projections from his coat pocket. Without a word, he tossed them into the empty grate.

‘Some things,’ he said quietly, looking around the still and ancient room, ‘are not assets. Some things are… sanctuaries.’ He put his arm around his daughter’s shoulders. ‘And we will keep it just as it is. We will protect it.’

From that day on, Canterville Chase held a new meaning for them all. It was no longer the site of a famous haunting, or a piece of problematic real estate. It was a monument to a love that had defied convention, a love that had been tragically misunderstood, and a love that had finally been redeemed. It was not a diary of daily events, but a series of poems and meditations, the outpourings of a soul in deep and inconsolable pain. It was the voice of Lady Eleanor de Canterville.

She described the world as a grey and tuneless place, and life as a cage from which she longed to be free. The birth of her children had brought not joy, but a deeper terror, a fear that she would pass her shadow on to them.

I have asked the priests, and they pray for me, but God does not listen. There is but one cure for my affliction, and its name is Death. It is the only garden where I might find peace.’

The room was utterly still, the only sound Virginia’s soft, sad voice. She turned a few more pages, her fingers gentle on the brittle paper.

‘He has finally understood,’ she read on. ‘My beloved, my heart, my Simon. He weeps, for he does not wish to be my gaoler in this life any longer. He has read the poets who say that love is stronger than death, and he believes he can love me even there. Tonight, when the moon is hidden, he will give me the gift I have so long begged him for. He will open the door for me. It is not a sin, he says, but an act of the most profound and terrible love. He will unlock my cage and let the tired bird fly free. And he has sworn he will not linger long behind me.’

Virginia looked up, her face a mask of stunned revelation. ‘He didn’t murder her,’ she whispered. ‘He helped her. It was… a mercy.’

She read the final entry, dated only a day later. The script was ragged, almost illegible. ‘Her brothers have come. They do not understand love; they understand only property and honour. They call me murderer. They have taken my sword, and they have locked me in the little room behind the wall, without food or water, to think upon my ‘sin.’ But I do not think of sin. I think only of her, and of the peace upon her face. I am not afraid. Soon, I will be with my Eleanor in the Garden of Death.’

The book fell from Virginia’s fingers onto her lap. The secret of Canterville Chase was not a simple, brutal murder, but a tragedy of love and despair so deep it had echoed for three hundred years. Sir Simon’s sin was not just the taking of a life, but the terrible, loving choice that had damned him, a choice for which he could find no forgiveness until a little girl had wept for him, not knowing the true depth of what she was weeping for.

No one spoke. Even the twins were pale and subdued. The silence was finally broken by Mr. Hiram B. Otis. He took off his spectacles and wiped them, though there was no dust upon them. He looked at the little book, at the dried flower, and then at his daughter, whose face was illuminated by a kind of sorrowful wisdom.

‘Virginia,’ he said, and his voice was thick with an emotion she had never heard in it before. ‘My dear girl. You were right.’ He walked over to the great fireplace and took the bundle of architectural plans and financial projections from his coat pocket. Without a word, he tossed them into the empty grate.

‘Some things,’ he said quietly, looking around the still and ancient room, ‘are not assets. Some things are… sanctuaries.’ He put his arm around his daughter’s shoulders. ‘And we will keep it just as it is. We will protect it.’

From that day on, Canterville Chase held a new meaning for them all. It was no longer the site of a famous haunting, or a piece of problematic real estate. It was a monument to a love that had defied convention, a love that had been tragically misunderstood, and a love that had finally been redeemed. And in the profound, unshakable peace that now filled its halls, the two sad lovers, Sir Simon and his Lady Eleanor, were at last, and forever, at rest.

The great logs in the fireplace had been lit, but they seemed to give off more shadow than warmth, and the family sat in a circle of lamplight, a small island in a sea of ancient gloom. Mrs. Otis had ceased her weeping, and now sat holding her husband’s hand, her gaze fixed upon the door as though by sheer force of will she might summon her lost daughter through it. The Duke of Cheshire, who had refused all food, paced back and forth before the long windows, stopping every so often to peer out into the impenetrable blackness of the park, his young face a mask of misery.

It was close on midnight when a sudden sound broke the heavy stillness. It was not a ghostly clang or a spectral footstep, but something far more strange and unfamiliar in that house: the sound of a key turning in a lock, followed by a faint creak from the wall beside the great chimney-piece. Every head turned. Mr. Otis rose to his feet, his hand instinctively going to his pocket where, in a more civilised country, a revolver might have been. The panelling, a section of the wall they had never before noticed had any seam, swung slowly inwards, revealing not the black cavern Virginia had seen, but a soft, internal radiance, like the first light of dawn.

And in the centre of that light stood Virginia.

She was very pale, and there was a curious serenity in her large blue eyes. In her hands she held a small, antique casket, exquisitely wrought of silver and ivory. For a moment, no one moved or spoke. They simply stared, as if at an apparition more startling than any ghost. It was the little Duke who broke the spell. With a cry that was half a sob and half a shout of joy, he rushed forward. ‘Virginia!’ he cried, ‘Oh, Virginia, you are safe!’ He would have swept her into his arms, but he stopped short, checked by the strange, solemn light that seemed to emanate from her.

Mrs. Otis gave a faint scream and hurried to her daughter, enveloping her in a frantic embrace. ‘My child! My darling girl! Where have you been? We have been out of our minds with worry! You were taken by the gypsies, we were sure of it!’

‘I have not been far,’ said Virginia, in a voice that was quiet and clear as a little bell. ‘I have been with the Ghost. He is at peace now.’ She looked at her father, who had approached more slowly, his practical American mind struggling to process the scene before him. ‘He asked me to give you this.’

She held out the casket. Mr. Otis took it, turning the small, heavy box over in his hands. It was unlocked. He lifted the lid, and the whole family peered inside. There, resting on a bed of faded purple velvet, was a collection of magnificent jewels. Ropes of pearls, diamonds that glittered like frozen stars, and fiery rubies that seemed to still hold the warmth of some long dead sun. There were rings and brooches and a great necklace of emeralds that was worthy of a queen.

‘Good heavens,’ murmured Mr. Otis. ‘They must be worth a fortune. These are the Canterville jewels, the ones that were lost.’

‘They are his gift,’ Virginia explained simply. ‘He said that as my family had given him his rest, he wished to give me my dowry.’

The Duke of Cheshire blushed a furious scarlet, and looked from the jewels to Virginia and back again, his heart beating a frantic tattoo against his ribs. Mrs. Otis, for her part, was torn between a mother’s relief, a woman’s admiration for fine jewellery, and a deep-seated suspicion of any gift that came from a spectre. ‘But, Virginia, my dear,’ she said, her voice trembling slightly, ‘is it quite proper to accept jewels from… from a gentleman of his description? I do not know what Mrs. van der Luyten would say.’

‘I think, my dear, that in this case we may make an exception to the ordinary rules of etiquette,’ said Mr. Otis dryly, a faint smile playing on his lips. He looked at Virginia, and the smile faded, replaced by a look of profound seriousness. ‘He is truly gone, then?’

‘He is gone,’ she affirmed. ‘He is in the Garden of Death. I saw him there. He is with his Eleanor.’ She could say no more, as the memory of the sad, skeletal figures and the final, peaceful smile of Sir Simon brought tears to her eyes. She hid her face on her father’s shoulder, and he held her close.

‘Then he is at peace,’ Mr. Otis said softly, ‘and it is all thanks to my brave little girl.’

The practicalities of the situation, however, could not be ignored for long. ‘There remains the small matter,’ Mr. Otis announced, after settling his wife and daughter on the sofa, ‘of the telegrams I have despatched to every police inspector in the county, and, I believe, to Scotland Yard. I have reported a kidnapping by a band of gypsies.’

The twins, who had been examining the jewels with wide-eyed wonder, looked up with interest. This promised to be more entertaining than any ghost.

‘What will you tell them, Papa?’ asked Washington, who had a budding appreciation for the finer points of diplomatic maneuvering. ‘We can’t very well tell them the truth.’

‘The truth, my boy, is a commodity to be used with discretion,’ replied his father. ‘I shall inform them that there has been a most fortunate misunderstanding. I shall explain that my daughter, in a fit of youthful curiosity, discovered a secret passage within the house and, becoming trapped, was unable to make her presence known until now. It is an old house; such things are to be expected. It is perfectly plausible.’

‘And the gypsies?’ asked Cecil, the little Duke.

‘I shall send them a handsome apology and a donation for their trouble,’ said Mr. Otis. ‘It is the least I can do after having their camp turned upside down and their good name slandered all over the county. An American,’ he added, with a twinkle in his eye, ‘always pays his debts, even those incurred by a phantom.’

And so it was that the great Canterville Chase disappearance, which had promised to be the most thrilling mystery of the season, was resolved in a most disappointingly mundane fashion. The police were recalled, the gypsies were compensated, and society was left with nothing more to gossip about than the carelessness of American children in historic English manors. A few romantic souls, however, maintained that the little Duke of Cheshire’s devotion had been the real key to the affair, and that he had single-handedly rescued Miss Otis from a fate worse than death, a version of events which Cecil, for all his honesty, did not feel compelled to vigorously deny.

The following morning, the sun streamed through the great oriel window of the library, illuminating a room that felt strangely and wonderfully different. The oppressive chill that had always lingered in the air, even on the warmest of days, was gone. The shadows in the corners seemed less deep, the ancient oak panelling looked warmer, and a profound and unshakable peace had settled over the entire house.

The first to notice the most significant change were the twins. With a shared instinct, they rushed to the spot by the fireplace where the famous bloodstain had for so long defied all of Mrs. Otis’s modern cleaning agents. It was gone. Not faded, not scrubbed away, but utterly and completely vanished, as if it had never been. The floorboards were as clean and unblemished as any other part of the room.

‘Well,’ said the one called Stars, in a tone of distinct disappointment, ‘I suppose the fun is over.’

‘It’s no use,’ sighed Stripes, kicking disconsolately at the now immaculate floor. ‘The house has become respectable. It’s as dull as a Sunday sermon.’

They spent the rest of the morning attempting to rig a suit of armour to fall with a clatter upon the butler as he passed, but their hearts were not in it, and the wire kept slipping. The very spirit of mischief seemed to have departed with the Ghost.

Virginia, however, felt the change as a quiet joy. She did not join the family for breakfast, but slipped out into the gardens. A heavy dew lay upon the grass, and the air was sweet with the scent of damp earth and roses. She walked towards the east corner of the Chase, where a gnarled and withered almond tree stood, a tree that the gardener had pronounced dead for the last twenty years. As she drew near, she stopped, a gasp of wonder on her lips.

The barren almond tree, which had been nothing but a skeleton of dry, black branches, had burst into bloom. It was covered in a cloud of delicate white blossoms, so pure and lovely they seemed to have been spun from moonlight and silver. They shone in the morning sun, a testament to the prophecy fulfilled, a final, beautiful message from the other side of the veil. Virginia reached out and touched one of the blossoms, and as she did, she felt a peace settle in her heart that she knew would never leave her.

Later that day, the Duke of Cheshire found her in the long gallery, looking at the rather forbidding portraits of the Canterville ancestors. He was still in a state of considerable agitation, torn between his joy at her safety and his bewilderment at the events he could not comprehend.

‘Virginia,’ he began, his voice earnest and a little shy, ‘I have been thinking. About the jewels, I mean.’

‘They are very beautiful, are they not?’ she said, her eyes still on the portrait of a lady with a ruff and a discontented expression.

‘Beautiful, yes, of course, but it is what the Ghost… what Sir Simon said. About a dowry.’ He took a deep breath. ‘Virginia, you know how awfully fond I am of you. I have been ever since that first day at croquet. And when you were gone, I thought I should go quite mad. The world was utterly grey and pointless.’ He moved to stand beside her, taking her hand. It was no longer cold as it had been the night before, but warm and alive. ‘I don’t understand what happened yesterday. I don’t suppose I ever shall. It is like something out of a book of legends. But I do not care. I only care that you are here. Virginia, will you… will you let me speak to your father again? This time, I do not think he will say we are too young.’

Virginia turned to look at him, and for the first time, a real, bright smile lit up her pale face. The solemn, otherworldly wisdom in her eyes was softened by a very human happiness. She had faced the mysteries of Death, but it was Life and Love that were now before her.

‘Yes, Cecil,’ she said softly. ‘You may speak to him. And I think you will find he is in a very agreeable mood.’

Their engagement was announced a few weeks later, and was the talk of London society. Everyone agreed it was a most suitable match, uniting as it did the ancient lineage of the Dukedom of Cheshire with the fabulous, if rather recent, fortune of the American Otises. The wedding itself was a grand affair, held the following spring at St. George’s, Hanover Square. Virginia made a lovely bride, and wore the great Canterville necklace of emeralds, which shone against the white of her dress with a light that seemed almost alive. Lord Canterville, who gave the bride away, was in high spirits, having at last offloaded his ancestral home and still managed to see its famous jewels remain connected to the aristocracy.

After the wedding, Mr. and Mrs. Otis decided to remain in England. The Minister found he had grown rather fond of the English, for all their illogical reverence for the past, and Mrs. Otis had discovered that, without a ghost to contend with, country life was extremely pleasant. The twins were sent to Eton, where their ingenuity and American spirit caused a series of minor revolutions in the established order of things, and they were, on the whole, extremely popular.

Canterville Chase itself was never sold. It became the country home of the young Duke and Duchess of Cheshire, a place of light and laughter. Yet it never entirely lost its air of mystery. Visitors would often remark on the extraordinary peace that pervaded the old house, a stillness that was deeper than mere quiet. Sometimes, on a summer evening, as the young couple walked in the garden, they would pass the almond tree, which bloomed with a miraculous fervour every year, regardless of the season. And they would pause, and Cecil would hold his wife’s hand a little tighter, and they would look at the beautiful blossoms and then at the old grey towers of the Chase, silhouetted against the twilight sky. It was life, messy and unpredictable. And his wife, his beloved Virginia, seemed to be drifting away from it, into the perfect, unchanging stillness that had claimed their home. That night, when the house was quiet, he went to her. She was brushing her hair before the mirror, the candlelight making a halo of her head. ‘Virginia,’ he said, his voice hoarse with a fear he could no longer contain. ‘We cannot stay here.’ She turned, her blue eyes wide with surprise. ‘Not stay here, Cecil? But it is our home. It is so peaceful.’ ‘It is too peaceful!’ he burst out, the words tumbling over each other. ‘It is not natural. Nothing changes here. The flowers do not wilt, the food does not spoil, the dust does not fall! And you… Virginia, you are not changing either. It is as if you are frozen in time, like one of the figures on the tapestry.’ A flicker of something, perhaps memory, perhaps pain, crossed her features. ‘The Ghost,’ she whispered, ‘he wanted to forget time. To be at peace.’ ‘Yes,’ Cecil said, kneeling beside her and taking her hands. They were cool, so very cool. ‘But we are not ghosts, my love. We are alive. To be alive is to change, to grow old, to have wrinkles and grey hair. To see our son grow up and have children of his own. That is our peace, the peace of life. This… this is the peace of the Garden of Death.’ Virginia’s eyes filled with tears, real, hot, human tears. It was the first time he had seen her cry since the birth of their son. ‘What have I done?’ she sobbed, hiding her face in his shoulder. ‘I only wanted to help him. I asked the Angel to have mercy.’ ‘And he did, my love, he did,’ Cecil soothed, his own heart breaking for her. ‘You did a brave and beautiful thing. But the house… the house seems to have misunderstood. It has learned the lesson of peace too well. It has forgotten the lesson of life.’ They left the next morning. Mr. Otis, when consulted via a lengthy telegram, was, for once, at a loss for a practical solution, though he did suggest a thorough airing and a team of ‘vigorous American charwomen’ might be of some help. Mrs. Otis was simply glad to have her daughter away from that ‘drafty, morbid old place’. Lord Canterville, however, took the matter far more seriously. Cecil sought him out at his club in London, and laid out the whole fantastic story. The old aristocrat listened intently, his face growing paler with each detail. ‘Good heavens,’ he muttered when Cecil had finished. ‘I had always feared something of the sort. There are stories, you know, legends in the family that are not written down. The prophecy on the window was only the most public of the portents.’ ‘What do you mean?’ Cecil asked, leaning forward. ‘The Canterville peace,’ Lord Canterville said, lowering his voice, ‘was always a double edged sword. The prophecy speaks of the house being still. We all assumed it meant quiet. Free of clanking chains and bloodstains. But the older texts, the ones my grandfather kept locked away, speak of the Stasis. They say that when the curse of the restless spirit is lifted by an act of perfect love and perfect pity, the house itself would find its own rest, an eternal Sabbath. It would become a monument to the peace it had been denied for so long.’ ‘A monument?’ Cecil repeated, horrified. ‘A tomb. And anything left within its walls would become part of the monument. Preserved. Perfect. And dead to the flow of time.’ He stood up and began to pace the room. ‘This is my fault. I sold you the house, I should have warned you. But I thought it was all superstitious nonsense!’ ‘It is not your fault,’ Cecil said firmly. ‘The only question is, what do we do now?’ Lord Canterville stopped his pacing and looked at the young Duke. ‘The house responded to your wife once. She is the golden girl of the prophecy. She won prayer from the lips of sin. She is the key. But what the prophecy did not account for, what none of my ancestors could have imagined, was that the golden girl would wish to stay. They assumed she would be a visitor, a catalyst who would then depart, leaving the house to its eternal quiet. For her to live there, to bring new life into it… it has created a paradox the old magic cannot resolve.’ For weeks, they debated. Scholars were discreetly consulted, ancient books were pored over, but no answer presented itself. Meanwhile, away from Canterville Chase, Virginia began to change. Colour returned to her cheeks. She laughed again, a real, bubbling laugh that made Cecil’s heart ache with love. She developed a magnificent appetite, and complained about a dress being too tight. She was, in short, becoming wonderfully, beautifully, humanly imperfect again. They decided they would have to sell the Chase. It was a painful decision, but there seemed no other choice. It would be closed up, left to its silent, timeless peace. Yet the thought of it troubled Virginia deeply. ‘It feels like a failure,’ she said to Cecil one evening, as they sat looking out over the bustling London street from their townhouse. ‘Sir Simon is at peace, but his house is not. It is just… stopped. It is not the same thing.’ It was then that the idea came to her. It was so simple, so audacious, that it took Cecil’s breath away. ‘We must go back,’ she said, her eyes shining with a new, determined light. ‘One last time.’ ‘Virginia, no!’ ‘Listen to me, Cecil. When I was in that dark place with Sir Simon, I begged for mercy for him. I spoke of his suffering, his desire to sleep. I asked the Angel of Death to grant him the peace he craved, the peace of nothingness. But I am not him. I do not want that peace. I want your peace, my love. I want William’s peace. The peace of waking up, of seeing the sun, of a scraped knee and a burnt piece of toast. The peace of life.’ ‘What will you do?’ he asked, his fear warring with his admiration for her courage. ‘I will speak to the house,’ she said simply. ‘I fulfilled the first part of the prophecy. Now I must add a condition of my own. It is what my father would call, I believe, a contractual amendment.’ Their return to Canterville Chase was very different from their departure. They came not in flight, but with purpose. They left little William with his grandparents, and journeyed to the house alone, just the two of them. As they walked up the grand staircase, the silence pressed in on them, thick and heavy. The perfect, unblemished rose was still in its vase. ‘I will do this alone,’ Virginia said, kissing Cecil at the door of the Tapestry Chamber. ‘But be near.’ He nodded, his hand on the doorknob, a silent sentinel. Virginia walked into the centre of the room. She looked at the huntsmen, forever poised to sound their horns. She looked at the spot where the wall had faded away like mist. She closed her eyes. She did not need to see the dark cavern; she had carried it in her memory. ‘I am speaking to you,’ she said, her voice clear and steady, not loud, but filled with an unshakeable conviction. ‘To the spirit of this house, and to the memory of Sir Simon de Canterville. You were granted the peace you craved. But the price of that peace has become the stillness of death for all within these walls. That was not my prayer. That was not my wish.’ She took a deep breath. ‘I wept for your sins because you had no tears. Now, you must rejoice for my life, because it is full. I forgave life for its sorrows on your behalf. Now you must embrace it, for my sake, with all its changes and its imperfections. The prophecy is fulfilled, but it is incomplete. Let the house be still from haunting, but let it be alive with living. Let peace come to Canterville, not the peace of the grave, but the peace of a home.’ For a long moment, there was only silence. A silence so profound, so absolute, it seemed the house was considering her words. Then, a sound. A tiny, shuffling, scratching sound. Virginia opened her eyes. A small grey mouse had scurried out from behind the wainscoting and was now boldly nibbling at a fallen crumb on the floor, a crumb that could not have been there an hour before. Then, another sound. A soft, sighing creak from the floorboards above. From the hallway, a faint, metallic whirring, followed by a single, resonant chime. Bong. The great clock in the hall was striking the hour. A gentle breeze, the first she had felt indoors for years, stirred the heavy tapestry, and for an instant, it seemed as if one of the little huntsmen had finally lowered his horn. A single petal detached itself from the perfect white rose on the writing-desk and drifted silently to the floor. Virginia began to weep, but this time, her tears were of pure, unadulterated joy. The door opened and Cecil was there, his face a mask of anxious hope. ‘Did you hear it?’ she cried, laughing through her tears. ‘The clock! A mouse! Oh, Cecil, I think the house has agreed to our terms!’ He swept her into his arms, and at that moment, a sunbeam, which had been trapped, unmoving, on a patch of the floor for what seemed like an eternity, shifted. It crept across the boards and illuminated a cloud of dancing dust motes, each one a tiny, sparkling testament to the beautiful, glorious return of time itself. Canterville Chase was never still in that way again. It became a house of joyous noise, of running children, for William was eventually joined by a sister and another brother, and of laughter. It was a house where flowers wilted and were replaced, where clocks needed winding, and where dust had to be constantly battled by a staff of very vigorous, and very well paid, charwomen. The peace of Canterville remained, but it was a different kind of peace now, a living, breathing contentment. And sometimes, when Virginia, Duchess of Cheshire, now a handsome woman whose face showed the lovely map of a life fully lived, would walk in the garden, she would look up at the old grey towers, and she would smile. For she knew that she had not only saved a ghost, she had saved a house, by teaching it the simple, profound truth that the greatest peace is not one that ends life, but one that makes room for it.
